Here is the thing nobody tells you about conferences. Whatever you bring back has about three weeks of life in it, and then it is gone. Not refused, not rejected, nobody ever says no to you. It just stops being in anybody's head, including yours, and four months later you find the notes and you cannot remember why that company seemed so interesting. So this is what I do in the first week, and it is very boring. I narrow the list down to three. Not eight, not five, three. Then I put two dates in the calendar, with real people invited, because a date in a calendar survives an enthusiasm and a good intention does not. And I recommend avoiding the long report. Nobody asked you for a report, and writing it will take you the week you should have spent booking the meetings. The real test of a conference is not how many people you met. It is how many of them are still in your calendar in March.

I met about ninety people that week, and I am not a machine, so let me tell you honestly how the list gets shorter. In the first three days, before I forget who was who, I go through everything and I narrow it down to maybe eight names. What keeps somebody on my list is very simple. They named a gap they had already measured, and they gave me a date. That is it. Those two things tell me they are allowed to spend money and that somebody inside expects an answer. What gets somebody removed is the sentence I hear forty times a week, which is that they are interested in exploring a partnership. I am also interested in exploring a partnership. It costs nothing to say and it commits nobody. And one more thing, because it happens constantly with people who are polite. They apologise for being direct. Please stop apologising. Being direct is exactly what lets me plan my own quarter, and I have never once been annoyed by somebody who told me what they actually needed.

Let me tell you what happens to your business case in the room you are not in, because people find this genuinely shocking. Somebody else reads it out. Badly. In about ninety seconds, between two other items, to people who have not slept. So the document does not have to be brilliant. It has to survive being summarised by a person who does not care about it. Write the first paragraph as though it is the only paragraph, because most weeks it is. Now, the three roles. There is the sponsor, who carries it when you are not there. There is the decision-maker, who signs. And there is the one stakeholder who can block it, and that is the one everybody forgets to map. People do the sponsor and the decision-maker beautifully and then get stopped by a person in risk they had not thought about. And the last thing, which is the hardest to accept. The calendar beats the argument. A brilliant case that arrives after the budget cycle has closed waits a whole year, and by then your vendor has found somebody else to be excited about.
